rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Your eyesight is much blurrier than a human's, and if you are a domestic dog, you see about a quarter of the fine detail a human sees. If you are a red fox, you read about 6 cycles a degree, and if you are an arctic fox, about 9, where a human reads about 30.
rows.note: Left out the claim that only three species are measured, since no record supports it. Dog figure is 20/75 Snellen turned into about a quarter of a human's 20/20. Red fox figure comes from ganglion cell maps.

rows.title: Sharpest spot
rows.text: If you are a domestic dog with a long skull, as in a wolf, you see most sharply along a band level with the horizon, and if your skull is short, like a pug's, you see most sharply in one spot in the middle. If you are a red fox or an Arctic fox, you have one spot of sharpest sight and a streak of sharp sight running beside it. Nobody has measured this in coyotes, jackals or the other wild relatives, so nobody knows which pattern you have.
rows.note: Left out the ganglion and cone density figures because they stay with the red fox and Arctic fox and have no comparison job here.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a domestic dog, a red fox or an arctic fox, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where humans have three. In the domestic dog, one kind senses light most strongly at about 430 nanometers, a violet-blue, and the other at about 555 nanometers, a yellow-green.
rows.note: Left out which colors look gray, since no record states it. Fox peak values cover only one pigment, so only the dog's two peaks are given.

rows.title: Field of view, dim light and depth
rows.text: If you are a domestic dog, your eyes take in an estimated 240 degrees around you, where a human's take in about 180, and what both eyes see overlaps across roughly 30 to 60 degrees. You also have more rod cells than a human, even in the center of your retina where a human has none, and a layer called the tapetum behind the retina, which was full-sized in 7 of 10 dogs examined. Nobody has measured the field of view of most wild relatives such as foxes and jackals, and nobody has measured how any of you judge depth.
rows.note: Left out the coyote night threshold (R3) and the dog and cat focusing range (R5, not a depth cue record) to keep the row short.
